hero.description: 20 questions to identify the warning signals in your relationship. Behavioural changes, emotional distance, secrecy: take stock in complete confidence.

section1.title: Why are you taking this test today?
section1.p1: If you're here, something is on your mind. Maybe a detail that struck you, an accumulation of small changes, or simply a stubborn intuition that refuses to go away. And rather than sitting alone with that doubt, you're looking for a concrete tool to see things more clearly.
section1.p2: This test is not a lie detector. It doesn't claim to prove anything. Its role is to help you put words to what you're observing, to organise what you feel and to assess objectively whether the signals you're picking up deserve to be taken seriously, or whether they have simpler explanations.
section1.p3: Whatever the outcome, remember that seeking to understand is an act of clarity, not weakness. What you feel counts, and it deserves to be heard.

section2.title: The 7 most common behavioural signals
section2.intro: Research in couple psychology identifies recurring patterns when a partner is involved in an outside relationship. These signs aren't proof, but their accumulation should put you on alert.
section2.pillar1Text: Changed passcode, screen turned over, notifications switched off, messages deleted. The phone becomes forbidden territory when it wasn't before. It's one of the most frequently cited signals in both accounts and clinical studies.
section2.pillar2Text: Recurring lateness, unplanned outings, sudden "work" weekends. It isn't the change itself that raises questions, it's the fact that it comes with vague or contradictory explanations.
section2.pillar3Text: Fewer deep conversations, less interest in your daily life, a gaze that seems turned elsewhere. The person is physically present but emotionally absent.
section2.pillar4Text: New clothing style, a sudden fitness push, a different fragrance. When these changes aren't linked to an identifiable event (a new job, a birthday), they can signal a wish to appeal to someone new.
section2.pillar5Text: Every question becomes an accusation, every remark provokes a disproportionate reaction. This permanent defensiveness is often a sign that the person feels "caught" and is trying to flip the guilt.
section2.pillar6Text: Small lies about harmless details, versions that change, timelines that don't add up. Taken one at a time, each seems trivial. Together, they trace a pattern of concealment.
section2.pillar7Text: Either a clear retreat (less affection, less desire), or on the contrary a sudden surge of attention and passion. Both extremes can reflect guilt or a need to compensate.

section3.title: Emotional infidelity vs. physical infidelity
section3.p1: When we talk about infidelity, we often picture a sexual relationship with a third person. But the reality is more nuanced. Couples therapists distinguish two main forms, both of which can be devastating for a relationship.
section3.sub1P1: It often begins with an intense friendship, shared confidences, a privileged bond with someone outside the couple. Your partner confides in that person what they no longer tell you. This form is more insidious because it doesn't necessarily involve physical contact, which makes it easier to deny: "We're just friends."
section3.sub1P2: Yet emotional infidelity can hurt as much as physical infidelity, sometimes more. It strikes at what the bond is built on: intimacy, sharing, exclusive closeness.
section3.sub2P1: More easily identified, it involves intimate contact with a third person. It can be a one-off (an isolated lapse) or long-running (a double life). In both cases, it's the breach of the trust contract that hurts, not only the act itself.
section3.sub2P2: Some studies suggest that men are more affected by physical infidelity, while women suffer more from emotional infidelity. But that distinction is a tendency, not a rule: the pain depends on each individual and each story.

section4.title: The psychology behind infidelity
section4.p1: Understanding doesn't mean excusing. But in order to move forward, whether you decide to stay or to leave, it can help to understand the psychological mechanisms behind infidelity.
section4.pillar1Text: The cause most often cited in therapy isn't sexual desire, it's the feeling of no longer being seen, heard or wanted within the relationship. Infidelity then becomes a clumsy search for emotional validation.
section4.pillar2Title: Fear of commitment or of routine
section4.pillar2Text: Some people unconsciously sabotage their relationship when it becomes too stable. The novelty of an outside relationship gives them a rush that offsets an existential anxiety about lasting commitment.
section4.pillar3Text: Infidelity can be a pattern that repeats from one relationship to the next. In that case the problem isn't the relationship itself, but a deep personal way of functioning, often linked to attachment style or family history. Our attachment style test can shed light on that dimension.
section4.pillar4Text: Turning forty, a bereavement, a job loss, the arrival of a child: these fragile moments can trigger a search for meaning that expresses itself through an outside relationship. That isn't an excuse, it's context worth taking into account.

section5.title: What to do if you suspect infidelity
section5.p1: The period of doubt is one of the hardest. The mind swings between the need to know and the fear of the answer. Here is what couples therapists recommend.
section5.dont1Text: Going through the phone, installing spyware, following your partner. Even if you find something, this approach poisons the relationship and can have legal consequences. It also locks you into a surveillance role that destroys your own peace of mind.
section5.dont2Text: Confronting your partner by shouting "I know you're cheating on me!" when you don't actually know will produce either a wall of denial or an escalation. A direct accusation closes the conversation instead of opening it.
section5.dont3Text: Confiding in one trusted friend is healthy. But exposing the situation to your whole family and your social networks before things are clarified makes any possible reconciliation considerably harder.
section5.do1Title: Observe, write it down, don't react in the heat of the moment
section5.do1Text: Take a step back. Note factually what you observe (dates, behaviours, inconsistencies). It will help you tell facts from your interpretations and structure your thinking.
section5.do2Title: Express what you feel without accusing
section5.do2Text: "For a few weeks now I've felt a distance between us and it worries me. I need us to talk about it." This approach opens the conversation instead of closing it. You aren't accusing, you're sharing a feeling.
section5.do3Text: A therapist, individually or as a couple, can help you get through this period. They will give you a neutral space to put words to what you're living and guide you towards the best decision for you.

section6.title: Can a relationship be rebuilt after infidelity?
section6.p1: The short answer: yes, in some cases. Studies show that roughly 50 to 60% of couples who choose to work on an infidelity manage to rebuild a satisfying relationship. But it takes a massive investment on both sides.
section6.sub1P1: The first condition is that the unfaithful person fully takes responsibility, without minimising, without blaming the other. The second is total transparency during the rebuilding period: open access to communications, honest answers to every question. The third is therapeutic work to understand the deeper causes and prevent a repeat.
section6.sub2P1: Therapists estimate that it takes between 1 and 3 years for a couple to find stable trust again after an infidelity. The first months are the hardest: the pain is raw, trust is at its lowest, and the betrayed person regularly relives the wound. That's normal, and it's essential that the unfaithful partner understands it without growing impatient.
section6.sub3P1: If your partner denies the facts despite the evidence, refuses to end the outside relationship, makes you feel guilty for their own choices or does it again, rebuilding isn't on the table. These situations point to a deep lack of respect that goes beyond the question of infidelity. Our toxic relationship test can help you assess the overall health of your relationship.

section7.title: When should you consider leaving?
section7.p1: Staying or leaving isn't a binary decision made in a day. But certain signs clearly indicate that the relationship can no longer work in its present form.
section7.p2: It's legitimate to leave when your partner refuses all responsibility and turns the guilt back on you, when the infidelity repeats despite promises, when your mental or physical health deteriorates (chronic anxiety, sleep problems, weight loss), when you stay only out of fear of being alone or out of obligation.
section7.p3: Leaving isn't a failure. Sometimes it's the bravest and healthiest thing a person can do. If the red flags in a man or the red flags in a woman are piling up, trust what you see.
section7.quote: You cannot save a relationship on your own. It takes two to rebuild, but only one to decide to protect themselves.

seo.faq1Q: How do I know if my husband is cheating on me?
seo.faq1A: The most frequent signs include a sudden change in behaviour around the phone (changed passcode, hidden notifications), unusual hours with vague explanations, growing emotional distance and excessive reactivity when you ask questions. No single sign constitutes proof, but their accumulation should put you on alert. This 20-question test helps you assess the situation objectively.
seo.faq2Q: What are the signs of emotional infidelity?
seo.faq2A: Emotional infidelity shows up as an exclusive closeness with someone outside the relationship: confidences, frequent messages, a need to share with that person rather than with you. Your partner may become distant, less interested in your conversations and more protective of their phone. The phrase "we're just friends" often comes up to play the situation down.
seo.faq3Q: Can a couple rebuild after cheating?
seo.faq3A: Yes, provided both partners sincerely want to. Roughly 50 to 60% of couples who choose to work on an infidelity succeed. The essential conditions are fully accepted responsibility, heightened transparency and therapeutic support. The process usually takes between 1 and 3 years.
seo.faq4Q: My partner has become distant, is that a sign of cheating?
seo.faq4A: Emotional distance can have many causes: work stress, depression, exhaustion, a personal crisis. It doesn't automatically mean infidelity. On the other hand, if that distance comes with other changes (secrecy around the phone, altered schedules, excessive reactivity), the overall picture deserves your attention. The best approach is still to talk about it directly with your partner.
seo.faq5Q: Should you go through your partner's phone when you have doubts?
seo.faq5A: Therapists advise against it. Going through your partner's phone locks you into a surveillance role that destroys your own peace of mind and poisons the relationship, whether you find something or not. It can also have legal implications. The recommended approach is to express what you feel directly: describe what you observe, what you feel and what you need, without accusing.
